topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; framework may require adaptation for Australian healthcare systems, which have different regulatory structures, funding models, and digital health priorities.
takeaways: Review identifies specific digital competencies needed in public health roles; use this to audit which AI-related skills gaps exist in your Australian health organisation and prioritise upskilling in priority areas.

European framework can inform curriculum design for health worker AI training, though you'll need to map it against Australian health policy, privacy legislation (Privacy Act, My Health Records), and sector-specific digital health roadmaps.

Scoping review approach suggests competency frameworks are best built iteratively across multiple roles and sectors — useful if designing AI literacy programmes across your health workforce rather than one-size-fits-all training.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on academic faculty in public health settings. Generalisability to other sectors, non-academic workplaces, or non-health disciplines unclear without access to full text.
takeaways: Faculty development programs can shift mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; design interventions that address concerns and build confidence rather than mandating adoption.
In public health contexts, structured capability-building for educators is foundational — train-the-trainer approaches may amplify AI literacy across student cohorts and organisational practices.
Identify and address specific barriers to AI adoption within your sector (e.g., ethical concerns in healthcare) to tailor literacy initiatives for relevance and uptake.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education context, but the framework's applicability to adult workplace learning and organisational settings is unclear without seeing full methodology and geographic scope.
takeaways: A holistic digital literacy framework that embeds AI competencies (rather than teaching them in isolation) may be more effective for foundational learning; consider how this 'integrated' approach might apply when designing AI capability programmes for employees with varying technical backgrounds.

Middle school curricula typically emphasise conceptual understanding and ethical reasoning about AI alongside technical skills — this balance could inform how you structure AI literacy for non-technical staff who need to understand AI's role and limitations in their roles.

articles.title: The AI perception gap: How to ensure employers and workers are ready for transformation | World Economic Forum - World Economic Forum
articles.snippet: The AI perception gap: How to ensure employers and workers are ready for transformation | World Economic Forum  World Economic Forum
articles.generalisability: Moderate — WEF reports typically draw on international surveys and expert panels, but specific sample demographics and methodology are not detailed in the snippet. Findings may skew toward developed economies and larger organisations.
takeaways: Identify and map the specific perceptions of AI capability and readiness held by leadership versus frontline staff in your organisation — misalignment here is likely driving resistance to AI adoption.
Design targeted communication and upskilling interventions that address the gap between employer expectations and worker concerns, rather than assuming a one-size-fits-all approach will work.

Use perception data to inform change management strategy: workers who perceive a gap between organisational AI ambitions and their own preparedness are at higher risk of disengagement during transformation.

articles.title: AI fluency: The next foundation of US economic competitiveness - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: AI fluency: The next foundation of US economic competitiveness  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: US-specific — focuses on US economic competitiveness, labour policy, and workforce development priorities that may not directly translate to Australian context, though core principles about AI fluency as a foundational skill may have broader relevance.
takeaways: AI fluency is positioned as a critical economic competency, not just a technical skill — consider how to frame AI capability development in your organisation beyond IT roles to build broader competitive advantage.

The whitepaper likely emphasises workforce-wide adoption; assess your current baseline of AI literacy across non-technical functions (HR, operations, finance) to identify upskilling priorities for your local team.

US-specific policy and grant schemes referenced in the report may not apply in Australia — focus on translating the underlying rationale for AI fluency investment into your own organisational business case.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis likely draws on global client work and industry trends, but specific case details and applicability to smaller organisations or non-corporate sectors not specified in snippet.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a standalone training initiative but as a core change management priority tied to organisational strategy and business outcomes.
Position AI literacy development as essential for managing resistance and enabling broader organisational transformation, not just technical capability-building.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be fully assessed from the title and snippet alone. The findings would depend on the study's sample composition, sectors included, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the information provided.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations has mixed effects on employee creativity — it can enhance some creative capabilities while constraining others, so implementation strategy matters more than adoption alone.

When rolling out AI tools, consider how they might reduce certain types of creative thinking (e.g., exploratory ideation) while boosting others (e.g., execution efficiency), and design role-specific adoption plans accordingly.
Monitor employee perceptions of AI as a creative constraint versus enabler during implementation, as these perceptions may influence engagement and actual creative output.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and whether findings apply beyond paternalistic leadership contexts. Paternalistic leadership is culturally variable — more prevalent in East Asian organisations — so applicability to Australian workplaces with different leadership norms requires consideration.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customising and shaping how AI is integrated into their workflows — this strengthens collaboration and reduces resistance to AI implementation.

Recognise that leadership style matters: paternalistic leaders may need to deliberately create space for 'AI crafting' (employee-driven adaptation of tools) rather than imposing top-down AI deployment, to activate the ownership mechanism.

When designing AI adoption programs, combine clear organisational ownership structures with opportunities for individual employees to personalise and craft their AI tools — this dual approach supports both alignment and engagement.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance perspective) is likely broadly applicable across sectors, but geographic scope and organisational types sampled are unclear.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations can trigger both approach behaviours (seeking new skills, expanded roles) and avoidance behaviours (defensive job narrowing) in employees — managers should anticipate and address both responses through targeted support and communication.

Job crafting is a key psychological mechanism through which employees respond to AI adoption; proactively helping staff reshape their roles and responsibilities during AI implementation may reduce resistance and enhance adaptation.
Understanding employees' psychological distance from AI (approach vs. avoidance mindsets) could help tailor upskilling programs and change management strategies to match individual readiness levels.

articles.title: Workers weather stress, uncertainty, and AI with psychological capital - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers weather stress, uncertainty, and AI with psychological capital  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — snippet provides insufficient detail on sample characteristics, geographic scope, or methodology. Appears to be a general APA resource rather than a primary research study, so generalisability cannot be assessed without full article.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) as a buffer against AI-related workplace stress — consider targeted interventions that develop these four dimensions in your team.
Use psychological capital assessments to identify which team members may be most vulnerable to AI-related uncertainty, then tailor support (mentoring, upskilling, or role clarity) accordingly.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The mechanism proposed (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) is theoretically sound but findings may vary significantly by industry, organisational culture, and implementation approach. Geographic scope unclear.
takeaways: Ethical leadership and psychological safety are critical buffers when implementing AI—organisations that fail to maintain these during AI adoption may inadvertently increase employee mental health risks.

Don't roll out AI tools without explicit focus on psychological safety; proactively communicate how AI changes roles, involve employees in decisions, and create channels for concerns about job security or ethical issues.

Monitor employee wellbeing during AI transitions as a key performance indicator—depression and disengagement may signal that implementation is eroding trust or perceived fairness, requiring course correction.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings on worker uncertainty; may not fully reflect Australian workplace contexts, industrial relations frameworks, or local AI adoption patterns. Applicable concepts around psychological responses to workplace change have some cross-cultural relevance, but specific policy and organisational references are US-centric.
takeaways: Acknowledge and name worker anxiety about AI and job security explicitly in team communications — uncertainty thrives in silence, and psychological safety improves when leaders validate concerns rather than dismiss them.

Create structured opportunities for employees to develop AI literacy and understand how their role will evolve, as uncertainty is often highest when workers lack clear information about how AI will be deployed and what skills will remain valuable.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's framework is based on consulting experience across multiple sectors, but specific client details and geographic scope are not clearly stated. Applicability may vary by organisational context and industry.
takeaways: Shift from 'AI adoption' framing (technology rollout) to 'AI adaptation' framing (behavioural integration) — this reframing helps teams focus on building sustainable human behaviours rather than just implementation metrics.
Design change interventions that explicitly target the specific behaviours your workforce needs to perform with AI tools, rather than assuming people will adapt naturally once systems are deployed.

Use Deloitte's change approach as a template to map the human capability gaps in your organisation before launching AI initiatives, allowing you to tailor training and support to actual behaviour change needs.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full methodology, generalisability cannot be assessed. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across contexts, but findings likely depend on organisational sector, AI implementation type, and employee demographics not evident from title alone.
takeaways: Job crafting behaviours shift when AI is introduced — some employees may actively reshape their roles (approach) while others withdraw or resist (avoidance). Understanding which employees fall into each category helps target support and role clarity interventions.

Frame AI adoption conversations around employee agency in task redesign. Employees who feel they can reshape their work around AI are more likely to adapt positively; those who feel threatened or powerless tend toward avoidance. Create structured opportunities for job crafting early in AI rollouts.

Monitor for approach-avoidance splits in your workforce — they're an early signal of uneven adoption and potential engagement issues. Use this framework to diagnose whether resistance stems from capability gaps, role uncertainty, or genuine job quality concerns.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings reflect primarily large organisations with resources for transformation programmes. Applicability may vary for smaller Australian organisations with different constraints.
takeaways: Design AI adoption programmes that treat workforce capability development as central to success, not a secondary implementation detail — this requires upskilling strategies tailored to different role types and career stages.

Anticipate and plan for behavioural resistance by identifying which employee groups face the greatest role disruption, then co-design transition pathways with them rather than imposing top-down change.

Embed psychological safety and clear communication about role evolution early in AI rollouts to reduce anxiety and build employee buy-in for behaviour shifts required to work effectively alongside AI tools.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without disclosed empirical data or specific geographic/sector focus. Insights may reflect Silicon Valley assumptions and may not generalise across industries, geographies, or organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify which routine tasks in your team are most vulnerable to AI displacement, then proactively reskill those employees into higher-value work (e.g. strategy, stakeholder management, complex problem-solving) rather than waiting for disruption.

Audit your current change management and communication practices: employees experiencing AI-driven role changes need clear narratives about how their skills remain valuable, not just assurances that 'jobs won't disappear'.

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics not evident from the title and snippet alone. If based on a specific population or sector, findings may not transfer universally across industries or geographic regions.
takeaways: Build self-efficacy around AI tools before rolling them out — employees with higher confidence in their ability to use AI report better mental health outcomes during adoption, suggesting pre-implementation training and gradual exposure reduce anxiety and resistance.

Monitor mental health as a key adoption metric alongside technical metrics — the connection between self-efficacy and psychological wellbeing means adoption programmes should include wellbeing check-ins and psychosocial support, not just skills training.

Tailor adoption support to individual confidence levels — recognise that self-efficacy varies; low-confidence employees may need one-on-one coaching, peer mentoring, or extended practice time to prevent mental health deterioration during AI integration.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, but specifics of sample size, sectors, and geographic distribution not stated in snippet. Findings likely reflect practices at large organisations with resources for AI investment.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI maturity across three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to identify capability gaps and prioritise interventions — rather than treating AI transformation as a single initiative.

Tailor change management and capability-building strategies to each horizon: early adopters may need foundational literacy and experimentation support, while mature programmes require focus on measuring ROI and embedding AI into core operations.

Use the three-horizon framework to communicate progress and reset expectations with stakeholders, reducing the gap between initial AI enthusiasm and realistic timelines for measurable business impact.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on a single neuroimaging study; sample size and methodology not detailed in snippet, so findings may not generalise broadly to all populations or clinical presentations of psychopathy.
takeaways: Brain imaging can detect structural or functional differences associated with psychopathy, suggesting it's not purely behavioural but has measurable neurological signatures.
Psychopathy appears to have a biological basis visible in brain scans, which challenges the idea that antisocial behaviour is entirely learned or chosen.
This kind of research is fascinating because it bridges neuroscience and psychology — showing how brain architecture might underpin personality traits we associate with moral decision-making.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the twin sample characteristics (likely US-based given PsyPost's typical coverage), which limits application to other populations and political contexts.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that authoritarian political beliefs have a heritable genetic component, suggesting personality and temperament differences matter more than commonly assumed in political psychology.

The finding that genetics partially explains authoritarianism is counterintuitive because political beliefs are often framed as purely learned or ideological—this suggests nature and nurture both shape how people respond to authority.

Understanding authoritarianism's roots in individual differences (not just social conditioning) helps explain why the same messaging resonates differently with different people, regardless of their upbringing.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — typical of news coverage summarising academic research, without detail on original study's sample size, geography, or methodology.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance, aggression, callousness) paradoxically attracts romantic partners in initial stages, likely because confidence and assertiveness read as attractiveness before the downsides emerge.

The finding is counterintuitive because we associate narcissism with relationship toxicity, yet the very traits that make someone a difficult long-term partner can be initially seductive — a mismatch between short-term charm and long-term compatibility.

This reveals an evolutionary puzzle: if antagonistic narcissists make terrible partners, why haven't we evolved better filters? The answer suggests our attraction heuristics are optimised for ancestral conditions, not modern relationship selection.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Findings suggest broad cross-cultural patterns in music-personality links, though specific musical genres and cultural contexts may vary by region.
takeaways: People with similar personality traits gravitate toward similar music genres worldwide—suggesting music taste is a surprisingly universal window into temperament, not just cultural preference.
Your Spotify playlist might reveal more about your openness to experience, conscientiousness, and emotional stability than you'd expect, across continents and cultures.
Music preference appears to tap into something fundamental about human psychology that transcends language, geography, and cultural background.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews research on MBTI across multiple studies, but findings may be limited by the quality and diversity of underlying leadership behaviour studies included in the analysis.
takeaways: Despite MBTI's massive popularity in corporate settings, it performs surprisingly poorly at actually predicting how people will lead — a disconnect between its cultural ubiquity and scientific validity.

The appeal of MBTI may lie more in its narrative satisfaction (people love their 'type') than its utility as a predictive tool, raising questions about why organisations keep investing in it for leadership development.
Better alternatives exist for assessing leadership potential; MBTI's stickiness in business may reflect marketing success rather than evidence-based effectiveness.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology details not provided. Generalisability depends on whether wine review data represents diverse populations and whether personality-language links hold across different beverages or cultural contexts.
takeaways: Wine review language reveals personality traits — an unexpected window into how people express themselves through product descriptions rather than traditional personality assessments.
AI can detect subtle personality signals in everyday writing that humans might miss, suggesting our word choices betray consistent patterns about who we are.

The finding is delightfully niche: the specific link between wine-tasting vocabulary and personality is counterintuitive and highlights how human behaviour shows up in surprisingly mundane places like online reviews.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The causal pathway (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) requires careful interpretation; actual scope and sector representation unknown.
takeaways: AI adoption alone does not cause depression — the pathway runs through psychological safety and ethical leadership. Leaders who implement AI without establishing psychological safety and modelling ethical AI use may inadvertently harm employee wellbeing.

Psychological safety is a critical intervention point: proactively build trust, encourage questions about AI systems, and create spaces where employees can voice concerns about AI's impact on their work without fear of consequences.

Ethical leadership during AI transitions matters as much as the technology itself. Transparent communication about how AI will affect roles, coupled with visible commitment to fair and responsible AI use, can buffer against negative psychological effects.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG practitioner report likely draws on global client work, but specific sample details, geographic scope, and methodology are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Findings may reflect practices across BCG's multinational client base but generalisability to smaller organisations or non-consulting sectors unclear.
takeaways: Psychological safety can reduce barriers to participation and voice across hierarchical or diverse teams — consider auditing who speaks up in your meetings and what conditions enable quieter team members to contribute.

Creating level playing fields through psychological safety may improve equity outcomes — implement practices like psychological safety briefings, normalising questions, and rewarding thoughtful dissent rather than status-based authority.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — appears to be a theoretical or empirical contribution, but geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be determined from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) may be a key lever for helping employees view AI tools as enablers rather than threats, potentially reducing anxiety and increasing psychological safety in AI-integrated roles.

Organisations should assess and strengthen employee psychological capital through targeted development when introducing AI systems, as it may predict which workers innovate with AI versus resist or disengage.

Leaders in algorithm-driven environments should create conditions that build confidence and agency in AI use — this framing could shift employee mindset from passive compliance with AI to active problem-solving partnership.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-specific — findings reflect American workplace conditions, labour market dynamics, and workforce demographics. Limited applicability to Australian workplaces, which differ in regulatory environment, employment culture, and organisational structures.
takeaways: Identify specific barriers to psychological safety in your team (e.g. fear of speaking up, blame culture, status hierarchies) by comparing your workplace against APA's 2024 findings, then design targeted interventions to address the most pressing gaps.

Use the report's data on psychological safety trends to make a business case to leadership for investing in safety initiatives — connect improved safety to measurable outcomes (retention, innovation, engagement) relevant in your Australian context.

Audit your current practices against the report's benchmark of psychologically safe workplaces: Do people feel safe taking interpersonal risks? Can they speak up without fear? Use this as a baseline for measuring progress over time.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM guidance is US-focused and may reflect US workplace norms, though psychological safety principles have broad applicability. Specific HR policies or legal frameworks referenced may not apply in Australia.
takeaways: Leaders can systematically build psychological safety through concrete practices such as modeling vulnerability, responding constructively to mistakes, and explicitly inviting input—not just creating a permissive culture.
Psychological safety requires active leadership behaviour; passive non-punishment is insufficient to encourage team members to speak up, take interpersonal risks, or challenge ideas.
Regular evaluation of team psychological safety (via pulse surveys or one-on-ones) helps leaders identify gaps and track progress, moving from assumption to measurement.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global case studies and client work, but lacks peer-reviewed validation and may reflect biases toward large organisations and McKinsey's client base.
takeaways: Psychological safety underpins effective AI adoption: create explicit norms that legitimise experimentation, questions, and 'safe failures' when learning AI tools to build team confidence.

Design onboarding and team practices that distribute agency widely (not just to AI 'champions') — pair structured training with low-stakes opportunities for people to exercise autonomy and see personal impact with AI.
Clarify role boundaries and decision rights upfront when introducing AI; ambiguity about who owns AI decisions erodes psychological safety and slows capability building.
